lorna-s-silence-2008.gazette: The camera stays on the shoulder and follows Lorna through Seraing, the Liège steel suburb the Dardenne brothers have been filming in for their whole career. Non-professionals fill the margins of the frame, there is no score, and nothing in the cutting tells anyone when to feel. The ending arrives at the same walking pace as everything before it.

the-class-2008.gazette: Bégaudeau taught the job before he played it, and the students in the room were students, cast out of a single Paris middle school and worked through a year of improvisation workshops. The dialogue was built from what the class actually said back. It won the Palme d'Or, the first French film to take it in twenty-one years.

the-passion-of-joan-of-arc-1928.gazette: Dreyer worked from the surviving minutes of the 1431 condemnation trial and put the judges' recorded questions back in their mouths. Months of interrogation were compressed into a single day, but the words are the record's words. The faces were shot without makeup and in close-up, so the transcript arrives attached to a body.
the-passion-of-joan-of-arc-1928.prism: The catch is whose paper it is. Those minutes were kept by the court that burned her, so the most faithful source available is also the prosecution's version, and every line of Joan's comes through the men transcribing her.

le-corbeau-1943.gazette: The letters came first from Tulle, where between 1917 and 1922 an anonymous hand mailed accusations through the town until it turned on itself. Clouzot restaged the phenomenon in 1943, financed by Continental, the German-owned studio operating in occupied Paris. At the Liberation the film was suppressed and Clouzot was banned from directing; the ban lasted two years.

the-last-emperor-1987.gazette: The script follows Puyi's own memoir, written after years in the Fushun re-education prison — which is to say the record it engages was itself produced under supervision. Bertolucci was granted permission to shoot inside the Forbidden City, the first Western production allowed in. A man crowned there as a toddler ended his life tending plants in a Beijing garden, and the film keeps both facts in the same frame.

who-framed-roger-rabbit-1988.gazette: Judge Doom's freeway scheme rhymes with an actual case. Through the 1940s a holding company called National City Lines, backed by General Motors, Firestone and Standard Oil, bought up streetcar systems across American cities, and in 1949 a federal jury convicted the backers of conspiring to monopolize the supply of buses and parts. Los Angeles' Red Cars were gone by 1961, and the freeway went in where the tracks had been.
who-framed-roger-rabbit-1988.prism: The film needed a melting cartoon demon to make the plot land, because a holding company with three corporate backers doesn't read as a villain on screen. That's the cost of the joke — the real version survived its own verdict, and it's the one that got the freeway built.

malcolm-x-1992.gazette: Lee built from the Autobiography, from Nation of Islam history, and from the FBI files that tracked Malcolm X until the night he was shot at the Audubon Ballroom in February 1965. The hajj sequence was filmed in Mecca by a Muslim second unit, a rare grant of access for an American production. Twenty-nine years after the film opened, two of the three men convicted of the killing were formally exonerated.

the-aviator-2004.gazette: The hearings, the crash and the flight are all on the record: Hughes testifying before Senator Brewster's committee in 1947, the XF-11 coming down over Beverly Hills the summer before, the Hercules lifting out of Long Beach Harbor that November and holding the air for about a mile. Scorsese graded the early reels to imitate two-strip Technicolor, then let the palette catch up with the decades. The flying boat never left the water again.

summer-palace-2006.gazette: Lou Ye took the film to Cannes in 2006 without clearance from China's film bureau, and the 1989 material — students moving through Beijing in the weeks before June 4 — was the reason clearance was never coming. The film was banned at home and Lou was barred from directing for five years. He shot his next feature in secret.
summer-palace-2006.prism: A five-year ban is a strange sentence for showing events the country lived through; the punishment is its own admission that the footage matters. And the students here aren't political heroes, they're distracted and in love, which may be the part that was hardest to allow.

the-assassination-of-jesse-james-by-the-.gazette: Jesse James was killed in St. Joseph, Missouri on 3 April 1882, shot in the back of the head by a member of his own gang while straightening a picture on the wall. Robert Ford was sentenced to hang, pardoned by the governor of Missouri within the day, and spent the following decade re-enacting the shooting on stage for paying audiences. He was shot dead himself in a Colorado tent saloon ten years later.

hunger-2008.gazette: The blanket protest, the no-wash protest and the strike itself are documented. Bobby Sands died on 5 May 1981, on the sixty-sixth day without food, and nine more men died before it ended in October. He had been elected to the Westminster Parliament while he was starving.

il-divo-2008.gazette: Andreotti was prime minister seven times and a defendant twice, and Sorrentino builds from the court record rather than around it — the Palermo Mafia case, the Pecorelli murder charge, the roll of dead investigators and journalists that runs under the opening. Italy's high court ultimately let stand a finding that he had consorted with Cosa Nostra before 1980, an offence by then too old to prosecute. He was still a senator for life when the film premiered, and he called it a piece of rascality.
il-divo-2008.prism: Time-barred is not the same as untrue, and the whole film lives in that gap: a complete record that convicts nobody. Sorrentino's answer is to shoot him as a figure of pure style, which is the one verdict no court gets to hand down.

milk-2008.gazette: Milk recorded a will ten days after his election, to be played only in the event of his assassination, and the tape runs through the film in his own voice. He and Mayor Moscone were shot at City Hall in November 1978; the jury came back with voluntary manslaughter and the sentence worked out to a little over seven years. Van Sant shot much of the film on Castro Street, in the storefront where the camera shop had been.

the-secret-in-their-eyes-2009.gazette: Argentina passed the Full Stop law in 1986 and Due Obedience in 1987, and between them the cases against the men who had done the disappearing were closed. Congress annulled both in 2003 and the Supreme Court struck them down two years later, reopening files that had sat dead for a decade and a half. Campanella's investigator works in the years when the paperwork simply stopped moving.

senna-2010.gazette: Kapadia assembled the film entirely out of footage that already existed — race broadcasts, onboard cameras, home video, drivers' meetings — with no interview ever shown on screen. Senna was killed at Tamburello on 1 May 1994, the day after Roland Ratzenberger died at the same circuit. Italian prosecutors charged members of his team with manslaughter; the proceedings ran more than a decade and ended with no one convicted.
senna-2010.prism: The cameras that made him a global figure and the cameras that recorded him dying were the same rig, run by the same broadcast operation, and the film can't use one without the other. Archive-only sounds like restraint, but it means every frame was shot for somebody else's purposes first.
